Impact Crater. A depression in a planetary surface caused by the violent collision of an asteroid, meteoroid, or comet, creating a characteristic circular depression with raised rims and ejected material. Impact craters are among Earth's most dramatic geological features and are found on every solid body in the solar system. Older surfaces like the Moon show dense crater populations spanning billions of years. Large impacts fundamentally alter planetary evolution, redistribute material across surfaces, and have episodically triggered mass extinctions on Earth.

Impact craters form from the sudden deposition of kinetic energy at collision. The impactor compresses rock instantaneously, creating a shock wave that excavates material far beyond the projectile's size. Impact structures scale with impactor energy. Small meteorites create simple bowl-shaped craters. Massive asteroid impacts create complex features with central peaks, terraced walls, and surrounding ejecta blankets.

The Moon displays hundreds of thousands of craters ranging from microns to thousands of kilometers across. Ancient crater densities are used to date lunar surface regions. Terrestrial impact craters include Chicxulub in Mexico, one hundred thirty kilometers in diameter, linked to the sixty-six-million-year-old extinction event that killed the dinosaurs. Vredefort in South Africa spans three hundred kilometers, the oldest known impact crater. Sudbury in Canada is one-point-eight-five kilometers across, a fossil complex impact with economic mineral deposits.

The giant impact hypothesis proposes that the Moon itself formed from debris ejected when a Mars-sized body collided with proto-Earth roughly four-point-five billion years ago. Ejecta, debris hurled from the impact site, blankets surrounding terrain and can contain shocked quartz and tektites, glassy objects formed from vaporized rock that cool mid-flight.

Impact crater density increases with surface age. Ancient highlands show more craters. Younger volcanic plains show fewer, allowing planetary geologists to estimate absolute ages of surfaces. On Earth, atmospheric entry friction causes most meteoroids to ablate before impact. Larger asteroids penetrate the atmosphere and produce craters. Oceans absorb most impacts without leaving permanent scars.

The Moon is the most densely cratered body in the inner solar system, preserving a four-point-five-billion-year record of impacts. The asteroid belt is the source of most impactors striking inner solar system bodies. The giant impact hypothesis proposes the Moon's origin from a planetary-scale impact. Large impacts can trigger climate change and mass die-offs, as in the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction. Mars is a heavily cratered terrestrial planet showing ancient and recent impact features.
